demographics.narrative:
New Zealand's estimated resident population was 5,357,300 at 30 June 2026, according to provisional figures, after growth of 36,400 people (0.7 percent) over the year.{{1}} Natural increase of 18,700 was the lowest since the early 1940s, and net migration added 17,600.{{1}} The median age was 39.3 years for females and 37.8 years for males.{{1}} At the 2023 Census, 67.8 percent of people identified as European, 17.8 percent as Māori, 17.3 percent as Asian and 8.9 percent as Pacific peoples, with some people identifying with more than one ethnicity.{{2}} About 84 percent of people live in urban areas.{{3}}

The population is aging. People aged 65 and over made up 17.6 percent of residents in 2025, the fertility rate was 1.57 births per woman in 2024, and life expectancy at birth was 82.0 years.{{4}}{{5}}{{6}} Māori and Pacific peoples have shorter life expectancy than New Zealanders of European ethnicity.{{7}} For a foreign academic medical center, this points to rising demand for chronic and age-related care in a small, high-income market served mainly by a tax-funded public system.

government.narrative:
New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy.{{7}} The Governor-General, Dame Cindy Kiro, represents the King, dissolves Parliament before a general election, appoints the government after it and signs legislation on the King's behalf.{{1}} Her term was due to end on 21 October 2026 but has been extended to 31 March 2027, so that appointing a successor does not clash with the election.{{2}} At the 2023 election National won 48 seats and ACT 11, so a National-led government needed New Zealand First's eight seats to secure a majority.{{3}} Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose National Party governs with ACT and New Zealand First, has set the next general election for Saturday, 7 November 2026.{{4}}

Health is run centrally. Simeon Brown is Minister of Health.{{5}} The Ministry of Health (Manatū Hauora) oversees the system and administers Vote Health, while Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) has planned and delivered public services nationally since 2022.{{6}}

economy.narrative:
New Zealand is a high-income economy, with GDP of about 305 billion international dollars at purchasing power parity in 2025, or about 57,350 per person.{{1}}{{2}} Services made up 74.4 percent of the economy in the year ended March 2024, goods-producing industries 20.4 percent and primary industries 5.2 percent.{{3}} GDP rose 0.2 percent in the June 2026 quarter, after a 0.9 percent rise in the March quarter, and grew 1.7 percent over the year ended June 2026.{{3}}

The Treasury's Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, presented on 29 September 2026, describes an economic recovery that has been delayed rather than derailed, first by the hit to confidence from United States tariffs in 2025 and then by the conflict in the Middle East.{{4}} Stronger tax revenue in 2025/26 left the deficit, measured as OBEGALx, $3.3 billion smaller than projected in Budget 2026, and the Treasury expects both OBEGALx and OBEGAL to reach surplus in 2028/29.{{4}} It warns that by 2030/31 New Zealand Superannuation and finance costs will take about 28 percent of the tax take, and that over the long term, unless checked, demographics will make the fiscal position unsustainable.{{4}} Projected financial improvements at Health New Zealand also help the fiscal outlook.{{4}}

facts.value: Ischemic heart disease, Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, stroke{{5}}

facts.label: Adults with high or very high psychological distress

disease_prevalence.narrative:
The Ministry of Health's mortality collection records 38,737 deaths in 2022, a preliminary figure.{{1}} Cancers caused 10,538 of them, ischemic heart diseases 4,607 and cerebrovascular diseases 2,275.{{2}}{{3}}{{4}} Measured by death rate, the leading causes in 2021 were ischemic heart disease (100 deaths per 100,000 people), Alzheimer's disease and other dementias (67) and stroke (46).{{5}}

Risk factors are widespread. In the 2024/25 New Zealand Health Survey, 34.2 percent of adults were obese, up from 31.3 percent in 2019/20, and 46.2 percent met physical activity guidelines.{{6}} Daily smoking fell to 6.8 percent of adults from 11.9 percent in 2019/20, though it remains 15.0 percent among Māori, and 11.7 percent of adults vaped daily.{{6}} One in six adults (16.6 percent) drank hazardously, and 14.3 percent reported high or very high psychological distress, up from 7.4 percent in 2019/20.{{6}} The burden points to sustained demand in cardiology, oncology, neurology and metabolic care.

public_system.narrative:
New Zealand gives permanent residents universal coverage through a system funded from general taxation and overseen by the Ministry of Health.{{1}} Eligible residents are covered automatically, hospital care is available at little or no cost at the point of use, and the Accident Compensation Corporation funds injury-related care.{{1}} The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 replaced the district health boards with a single national entity, Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora), and created a parallel Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora), which was disestablished in 2024 with its functions moved to Health New Zealand and the Ministry.{{1}} Most GPs work in self-owned clinics linked to primary health organizations; primary care is funded by capitation and hospitals through a diagnosis-related group model.{{1}}

Governance has been unsettled. A Commissioner, Professor Lester Levy, and deputy commissioners were appointed in 2024 to stabilize Health New Zealand, and in July 2025 the government re-established a board, with Levy as chair for 12 months.{{2}} Mark Darrow replaced him as chair for a three-year term from 1 May 2026.{{5}} In March 2025 Health Minister Simeon Brown said an independent Deloitte review showed the 2022 reforms were "rushed and poorly implemented," and he directed a shift to local decision making.{{3}} Access remains strained: in the 2024/25 Health Survey, 25.5 percent of adults cited the time taken to get a GP appointment as a barrier, and 14.9 percent did not visit a GP because of cost.{{4}} Hospital waits are improving against the government's health targets: in 2025/26, 72.6 percent of people received elective treatment within four months, up from 63.9 percent the year before, and 76.3 percent of emergency department patients were admitted, discharged or transferred within six hours.{{6}}

financing.narrative:
Current health expenditure was 10.1 percent of GDP in 2024, up from 9.2 percent in 2012, and about US$5,022 per person, according to World Bank data.{{1}}{{2}} Out-of-pocket spending was 12.7 percent of current health expenditure in 2024, and general government spending covered 77.7 percent in 2023.{{3}}{{4}} In 2023 New Zealand's share of GDP was slightly below Australia's and below Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States and the OECD average.{{5}} Pharmac buys medicines within a fixed budget, and prescription copayments are capped at NZ$5 per item.{{6}}

Budget 2026, released on 28 May 2026, provides more than $5.8 billion in new Vote Health operating funding over the forecast period, including a $1.37 billion annual uplift for cost pressures and demand, and the government says total health spending will reach $34.2 billion in 2026/27.{{7}} It funds 24,000 additional planned care treatments and 24,000 additional cancer treatments in 2026/27, among other services.{{7}}

facts.value: 42.1% of surveyed doctors; 43.5% of the register (2025){{1}}

workforce.narrative:
New Zealand had 20,530 practising doctors at 30 June 2025, up 2.6 percent on 2024, or 388.3 per 100,000 people.{{1}} International medical graduates made up 42.1 percent of doctors responding to the Medical Council's survey and 43.5 percent of those on the register, rising above 60 percent in Whanganui and South Canterbury.{{1}} Retention is the weak point: 99 percent of New Zealand graduates are retained after one year, against 40 percent of international graduates after two years.{{1}} Māori doctors make up 5.5 percent of the workforce and Pacific doctors 2.7 percent.{{1}}

World Bank data put physician density at 3.61 per 1,000 people in 2022, up from 2.71 in 2012 and above the OECD average of 3.43.{{2}}{{3}} Nurses and midwives numbered 12.3 per 1,000 people in 2023, and there were 2.51 hospital beds per 1,000 people that year.{{4}}{{5}} At 30 June 2026, 80,960 nurses held annual practising certificates, 4 percent fewer than a year earlier, and 43.5 percent of them qualified overseas.{{6}}

outlook.narrative:
Demand will keep rising as the population ages: people aged 65 and over were 17.6 percent of residents in 2025, up from 13.7 percent in 2012.{{1}} Policy is aimed at access and throughput. Budget 2026 adds a $1.37 billion annual uplift, funds more planned care, cancer treatment, emergency department events and general practice enrolments, and lowers the eligibility age for bowel screening to 56.{{2}} On supply, the Waikato medical school will add 120 places a year from 2028, and the Medical Council has shortened registration routes for overseas doctors.{{3}}{{4}}

The constraints are fiscal and structural. The Treasury projects the government's expense-to-GDP ratio falling below 30 percent by 2030/31 under tight future budget allowances, and it counts on financial improvements at Health New Zealand.{{5}} The public system runs on more than 4,000 fragmented information technology systems, and in 2024, 73 percent of New Zealanders said waits for doctors' appointments were too long.{{6}} The general election is on 7 November 2026.{{7}} Its result will shape how far elective surgery continues to be outsourced to private providers, which matters for any foreign partner weighing clinical or advisory work.

competitive_landscape.narrative: Foreign health systems have a small, mainly commercial presence in New Zealand. Icon Oncology Group delivers cancer care through Bowen Icon Cancer Centre in Wellington, a joint venture with Evolution Healthcare, and in early 2019 Bowen became the first Icon facility outside Australia to offer radiation therapy; Icon said in February 2025 that it had introduced clinical trials there.{{1}}{{7}} Evolution itself has been controlled by Australian investors since QIC agreed to buy it in December 2021.{{2}} US-based Sanford Health says it has collaborated with the Omni Health primary care network since 2018, and in July 2026 Health New Zealand signed an agreement with UCLPartners in London on digital and AI innovation.{{8}}{{9}}
competitive_landscape.closing: New Zealand is also a regional referral destination. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade funds the New Zealand Medical Treatment Scheme, which refers patients from Fiji, Kiribati, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu for treatment in New Zealand, Australia and Fiji.{{3}} In 2024, 53 people were treated overseas under its referral component.{{4}} Outbound, an industry publication reported in 2022 that it was common for New Zealanders to go to Australia for some treatment, and to Asia for dentistry, joint replacement and cosmetic surgery.{{5}} There is no official count of New Zealanders treated abroad, though agencies report rising demand, including for Türkiye.{{6}}

resolution_log: Not readable from this environment, so not cited: health.govt.nz HTML pages (403; its /system/files PDFs and DOCX were readable), rbnz.govt.nz, elections.nz and electionresults.govt.nz, dpmc.govt.nz, gg.govt.nz, teara.govt.nz, britannica.com, parliament.nz (JavaScript only), legislation.govt.nz (JavaScript only).

Health NZ private-sector outsourcing aide-memoire (tewhatuora.govt.nz) could not be opened, so outsourcing shares were not used; private hospital counts by group could not be reliably sourced, so the market chart uses World Bank hospital beds per 1,000.
Mortality: latest Ministry of Health cause-of-death counts readable were 2022 (preliminary) via Figure.NZ; 2021 death-rate ranking from the Commonwealth Fund profile. Percent shares were not derived.
Research pass 21 October 2026; three independent verifiers on the strongest model; points raised by only one verifier were re-checked on the source page in resolution.

Added: Health NZ board chair change (May 2026), 2025/26 health target results (Health NZ, October 2026), nurse workforce at 30 June 2026 (Nursing Council), first long-term private hospital contracts (NZ Herald, 2026).

Evolution Healthcare: the 2018 ownership article replaced; QIC agreed to buy it from PEP in December 2021, and it now lists six hospitals. Election sentence no longer cites a source for analysis. IMTJ outbound-travel item dated 2022.
English Language Act 2026 royal assent (5 August 2026) confirmed on Parliament's bill page.

Mortality kept at 2022 preliminary counts: Health NZ has published preliminary 2023 data, but only in a workbook that could not be read here. Fertility kept at the World Bank 2024 value (two newer Stats NZ figures were reported for different periods and not confirmed on a readable page).

Tracker: Penn State-Auckland excluded (general university partnership); Fiji National University-Otago/Mercy excluded (New Zealand institutions supporting a centre in Fiji); Sanford-Omni Health set to Unclear (the 2025 job posting could not be re-verified); Icon last evidence February 2025; NiPPeR follow-up records dated to the August 2025 completion; ZERO trial typed as research collaboration.
